title: Short Stuff: Speed Reading
summary: Short Stuff episode debunking speed reading. The hosts describe Evelyn Wood and her Reading Dynamics company, founded in the 1950s (first workshop 1959), which promised thousands of words per minute and taught "finger pacing." The episode covers its popularity with figures like JFK, Nixon and Charlton Heston, early criticism (a 1962 Saturday Evening Post piece called speed reading "bunk"), Marcia Biederman's book criticizing it, the Harvard Crimson's finding that the reading index comprehension tests got easier over time, a University of Missouri finding that comprehension scores were possible without reading the material, lawsuits against critics, and a cult-like faith framing. They close by citing Mark Seidenberg's explanation of reading fixations, which puts normal reading near 280 words per minute.
topics: Saturday Evening Post speed reading bunk

segments.title: Opening banter on the Internet and library research
segments.summary: Hosts joke about how long episodes would take without the Internet, then frame speed reading against the pre-search-engine era of card catalogs and skimming books. They introduce Evelyn Wood and Reading Dynamics and its claim of thousands of words per minute.

segments.title: Josh on his own reading pace
segments.summary: Josh says he reads slowly and deliberately, doubts claims of very fast reading, and distinguishes speed reading from skimming. He explains that Evelyn Wood said she taught reading, not skimming, using a technique called finger pacing that she called the greatest invention since the printing press.

segments.title: Commercial break
segments.summary: Hosts tease the upcoming segment on the scam of speed reading before a break.

segments.title: Popularity and early criticism of Reading Dynamics
segments.summary: Workshop claims of 5,000 to 7,000 words per minute are discussed, along with famous early adherents including John F. Kennedy, Richard Nixon and Charlton Heston. The hosts attribute the appeal to mid-century intellectual trends. A 1962 Saturday Evening Post article called speed reading 'bunk,' and the Washington Post later criticized the method.

segments.title: How the scam worked: rigged tests, faith and lawsuits
segments.summary: Marcia Biederman's criticism of finger pacing and the cost of the course is covered. The Harvard Crimson reported that the first comprehension tests were harder than the final ones, and a University of Missouri study found about 60 percent comprehension was possible without reading the material. The hosts also describe the faith-based, cult-like atmosphere, Wood's Mormon background, and lawsuits against critics.

segments.title: Why speed reading doesn't work
segments.summary: Mark Seidenberg's argument is summarized: reading happens through fixations of about a quarter to a fifth of a second, taking in roughly seven to eight letters each. That works out to about 280 words per minute, the average reading rate, so thousands of words per minute cannot be absorbed. The hosts also note that failed students kept quiet out of shame, and that speed reading ideas persist today.
topics: shame and silence among former students

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up that speed reading is not real and mention the show's production credit.
